title: The Morality of Suicide
rootClaim: An individual possesses absolute bodily autonomy and moral authority over their own life, making rational suicide morally permissible under specific circumstances.

branches.text: Bodily Autonomy & Self-Ownership: A competent adult owns their physical existence, granting them the ultimate right to choose when and how to end their life.

children.text: Mitigation of Intolerable Suffering: In cases of terminal illness or intractable agony, ending one's life is a rational act of self-compassion and dignity.
Depression & Cognitive Distortion: Severe psychological distress distorts rational decision-making capacity, rendering 'rational consent' illusory in acute mental crises.
Assisted Dying Safeguards: Palliative medical protocols mandate independent psychiatric evaluation, waiting periods, and terminal prognosis confirmation to ensure genuine rational autonomy.
Slippery Slope Objection: Legalizing assisted suicide incentivizes vulnerable, elderly, or disabled individuals to end life due to perceived burden on family or state budgets.
Stoic Rationality: Ancient Stoic philosophy (Seneca, Epictetus) posits that when life's conditions permanently prevent virtuous living, exiting life ('leaving the room') is morally acceptable.

branches.text: Duties to Others & Sanctity of Life: Suicide violates fundamental obligations to loved ones, society, and the intrinsic sanctity of human life.

children.text: Relational Harm & Social Contract: Suicide inflicts devastating psychological trauma, social disruption, and emotional grief on surviving family and community.
Asymmetry of Obligation: Obligating an individual to endure unbearable lifetime agony solely to spare others grief constitutes emotional coercion.
Kantian Categorical Imperative: Suicide treats one's own humanity merely as a means to escape discomfort, destroying the foundational agent of all moral value.

definitions.description: The right of an individual to govern their own body and make decisions about their personal physical integrity.
The practice where a physician provides a lethal dose of medication that the patient self-administers to end unbearable suffering.
Immanuel Kant's supreme moral principle requiring that actions be universalizable and treat humanity as an end in itself, never merely as a means.
The ancient Stoic doctrine that ending one's life is rational when physical or social circumstances render living virtuously impossible.
